description: In the K’iche’ Maya Popol Vuh, Xibalba is an underworld court reached by dark rivers and a crossroads that tests travelers before they arrive. Its death lords rule through humiliating trials — houses of darkness, blades, cold, jaguars, and bats — until the Hero Twins outwit every test, rise from their own ashes, and strip the lords of their honored standing, breaking the court’s old claim on the dead.

name: Polynesian / Māori Spirit Return (Hawaiki)
description: In Maori tradition the spirit travels the length of the land northward to Te Rerenga Wairua, the leaping place at Cape Reinga, descends by the roots of the ancient pohutukawa, and turns for a last look back before crossing the sea toward Hawaiki, the homeland the ancestors sailed from. Death runs the great migration in reverse: a wayfinding voyage home, with the living lineage as the wake the traveler leaves behind.

name: Aboriginal Australian Traditions (Return to Country)
description: Across hundreds of Aboriginal nations, death is widely understood as a return: the spirit goes back to the Country, waterhole, or sky-camp it came from, rejoining the ancestral order laid down in the Dreaming. The living walk it home with smoke, song, and mourning law — and the land itself remains the ancestor, present tense.

name: Naturalism (Mortal Oblivion)
description: The oldest rival to every map in this atlas: death as the end of experience. Epicurus taught that where death is, we are not; Lucretius added the mirror of the time before birth. Nothing crosses over — what remains is matter returned to the world, and the difference a life made while it ran.

name: Gnosticism (Ascent Through the Archons)
description: The soul is a spark of a higher world, held in matter by a lesser creator and his gate-keeping archons. At death the knower ascends, answering each archon with the words and seals learned in life, shedding the psyche's garments level by level, and rejoins the Pleroma — the fullness it fell from. Ignorance, not sin, is the enemy; gnosis is the road.

name: Chinese Ancestral Religion (Courts of the Ten Kings)
description: The most administered afterlife on record: the hun and po souls part at death, and the person passes through ten magistrate courts where deeds are read from ledgers and purgations served — while the living file appeals in the currency the courts recognize: offerings, spirit money, and the rites of a filial family. Lady Meng's broth of forgetting waits at the exit before rebirth.

name: Inca (The Three Pachas)
description: The Inca cosmos stacks three worlds: Hanan Pacha above, where the Sun receives the honored dead into warmth and plenty; Kay Pacha, this world; and Ukhu Pacha below, a cold inner country for the wicked. But the great dead never fully left — preserved as mallki, they kept their households, attended festivals, and were fed and consulted as seated members of the family.

name: Swedenborg (Heaven and Hell)
description: Emanuel Swedenborg's 1758 report from the other world: the newly dead wake in a middle country within days, met by angels, and nothing is sentenced — the externals worn in life fall away until the ruling love stands exposed, and each spirit migrates freely to the heaven or hell that matches it. Heaven is societies of similar loves, employed in useful work; every angel was once a person.

name: Manichaeism (The Return of the Light)
description: Mani taught that every living thing holds particles of stolen Light trapped in Darkness, and that salvation is a salvage operation. At death the Column of Glory lifts the freed light to the moon and sun, which ferry it home. Three roads open at the end of a life: the Elect go straight to the Light, the Hearers return to a body for another attempt, and those who refused go to the darkness. When the last particle is recovered, the cosmos burns and the Last Statue rises from what was saved.
origin: Mani in Sasanian Babylonia (c. 240 CE), spreading from North Africa to China

name: Mandaeism (The World of Light)
description: The last surviving Gnostic religion, still practiced by Mandaeans of southern Iraq and Iran and their diaspora. The soul is a stranger here, and death is the return trip. Three days after death it begins an ascent through the maṭarta — watch-stations where it is examined, detained, and cleaned of what it picked up in the world — a passage of some forty-five days that the living assist with the masiqta rite. At the threshold Abatur weighs it. There is no eternal hell: the stations purify rather than condemn.
origin: Mandaean communities of southern Mesopotamia and Khuzestan (formative 1st–3rd c. CE)

name: Latter-day Saints (Degrees of Glory)
description: Joseph Smith's 1832 vision replaced heaven and hell with a graded architecture in which nearly everyone is saved to some degree of glory. The dead wait in the spirit world — paradise or prison, with missionary work running between them — until the resurrection sorts them into three kingdoms named for the sun, moon, and stars. Only a handful, who knew and refused outright, go to outer darkness. Because the dead can still accept the gospel, the living perform baptisms on their behalf, which is why Latter-day Saints keep the world's largest genealogical archive.
origin: Joseph Smith, Hiram, Ohio (1832); the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints

name: Bahá'í (The Worlds of God)
description: The Bahá'í afterlife has no geography at all. Heaven and hell are not places but conditions — nearness to God and remoteness from God — and the soul, which comes into being at conception and does not return to earth, continues after death to progress through what Bahá'u'lláh calls the worlds of God, forever. The soul's state is compared to a bird released from a cage and to a child born out of the womb: the world it leaves was only the place it grew the faculties it will now need.

name: Apokatastasis (Universal Restoration)
description: The minority Christian tradition holding that hell is remedial and finite, and that God finally restores every rational creature. Origen argued in third-century Alexandria that punishment is corrective rather than retributive; Gregory of Nyssa held the same hope while abandoning Origen’s speculative machinery. The position was condemned in the sixth century — though scholars still dispute exactly what was condemned and by whose authority — and it has resurfaced in every century since.
origin: Origen of Alexandria (c. 230 CE) and the Greek and Syriac Fathers after him

name: BaKongo (Kalunga and the Turning)
description: In BaKongo thought the cosmos is a circle cut by a line of water. Above the Kalunga line is the world of the living; below it, reversed as in a mirror, the world of the dead. The sun does not stop at sunset — it crosses and goes on shining underneath, and a human life follows the same circuit through four moments: musoni, kala, tukula, luvemba. Death is not an exit but the far quarter of the turn, and the ancestors, the bakulu, remain in working relation with the village that keeps them.
origin: Kingdom of Kongo and BaKongo peoples of Central Africa (c. 1400 CE onward)

name: Haitian Vodou (Ginen and Anba Dlo)
description: A person is made of parts, and death takes them apart. The gwo bonanj and ti bonanj are separated from the body in the desounen rite, and the spirit goes anba dlo — under the water — where it waits a year and a day. Then the family performs wete mò nan dlo, taking the dead out of the water, and the spirit is drawn into a govi jar, brought back into the household, and set on the road to Ginen: Africa, the ancestral country beneath the sea. The dead who are served well may in time be raised among the lwa.
origin: Saint-Domingue and Haiti, from Fon, Yoruba, Kongo, and Catholic sources (from 1791)

name: Diné (The Chindi and the Turned Face)
description: The Diné account of death is a refusal of the whole genre. There is no reward, no paradise, and no realm anyone hopes to reach. What matters is the chindi — the residue left behind at the last breath, everything in a person that was out of harmony, which lingers and can sicken the living. The response is avoidance and containment: death outdoors where the chindi disperses, a dwelling abandoned if someone dies inside, the name unspoken. The work is not to secure a destination but to restore hózhó among the living.
origin: Diné (Navajo) of the American Southwest; documented traditional practice

name: Slavic (Nav and the Bird-Country)
description: Reconstructed from folklore, funerary practice, and language rather than from scripture, the pre-Christian Slavic dead go to Nav — the realm of the dead — while Vyraj or Iriy, the warm country beyond the sea or in the crown of the world tree, is where birds and souls winter. Souls linger forty days; birds carry and announce them; the drowned and the wronged stay behind as navki and rusalki. Grave-feasts kept the dead fed. The tidy three-realm cosmos often presented as Slavic is a twentieth-century invention.

name: Finnic (Tuonela Across the Black River)
description: Tuonela — also Manala — lies across a black river, and Tuoni’s daughter rows the dead over it. What waits is not fire and not reward: the good and the wicked arrive at the same grey place and continue as shadows, sleeping in Tuoni’s beds. Tuonetar meets the newcomer with a drink that takes the living world away. A black swan circles the water. The living stay in contact through lament — the itkuvirsi, sung by women, which guides the dead across and carries messages both ways.

name: Etruscan (Charun and the Banquet)
description: The Etruscans painted their tombs as dining rooms. The dead recline at a banquet with the family who went before them, wreathed and served, while at the doorway stands Charun — blue-skinned, hook-nosed, tusked, holding a hammer — and Vanth, winged, carrying a torch and a scroll. There is no weighing and no sentence: the demons are escorts and doorkeepers, not judges. Later tombs darken, and the road to Aita and Phersipnai fills with things that were not there before.

name: Plato (The Myth of Er)
description: At the end of the Republic, a soldier named Er dies, lies twelve days on the pyre, and revives to report what he saw. Souls are judged and sent up or down for a thousand years — tenfold repayment either way — then gather at a shaft of light where the spindle of Necessity turns. There the Fates set out lots and lives, and each soul chooses its own next life. Most choose badly, out of habit. Then all drink from the river of Forgetting and are shot out like stars into birth.

name: Orthodox Toll-Houses (Telonia)
description: In an account held by many Orthodox Christians and disputed by others, the soul spends three days near the earth, then ascends through the air past a series of toll-houses — telonia — where demons produce the record of a particular sin and the escorting angels answer with the good the soul did. What is not covered is seized. The soul is shown heaven and hell over forty days and receives a provisional verdict awaiting the general resurrection. The Church has never dogmatized it, and prominent hierarchs call it false.
origin: Byzantine and Egyptian ascetic tradition; formative from c. 400 CE

name: Conditional Immortality (Soul Sleep)
description: A Protestant minority position, held by Seventh-day Adventists, Jehovah’s Witnesses, Christadelphians and a growing number of evangelical theologians: the soul is not naturally immortal. The dead are unconscious — asleep, knowing nothing — until the resurrection. Immortality is a gift given only to the saved. The wicked are not tormented forever but destroyed: the second death is annihilation. And the reward is not a disembodied heaven but a renewed earth, physical and populated.
origin: Reformation-era conditionalism; formalized among Adventists and others from 1863
searchText: Death → unconsciousness, the sleep of death, with no experienced interval and no communication either way → resurrection → judgment → immortality conferred as a gift on the saved, who are raised bodily onto a renewed earth; the wicked destroyed in the second death rather than tormented endlessly. · Deep unlit rest with no interval in it, opening directly onto morning over an ordinary inhabited landscape. · Ecclesiastes 9:5; Psalm 146:4; 1 Timothy 6:16 · Edward Fudge, The Fire That Consumes (1982) · Seventh-day Adventist Fundamental Beliefs (25–28) · Rethinking Hell (contemporary evangelical conditionalism) · No conscious interval — the dead are nowhere · The resurrection as the next subjective moment · A renewed and physical earth · The second death, leaving nothing behind · No hell to be located · An unbroken dark with no duration in it · Ordinary morning light on farmland · A fire that goes out when it is done · Empty ground where a place would be · Houses built to be lived in · The sleeping dead · Edward Fudge · John Stott · The renewed earth

name: Spiritism (Kardec)
description: Allan Kardec organized the seance-room material of 1850s Paris into a system and published it as doctrine. Spirits are immortal, they reincarnate as many times as it takes, and the point of every life is moral progress — never punishment. Between lives comes erraticity, a wandering state in which the spirit reviews what it did and helps plan the next attempt. There is no hell and no eternal damnation; suffering is remedial and self-inflicted. Brazil took it seriously, and it is now a mass religion there.
origin: Allan Kardec, Paris (1857); mass following in Brazil

name: Theosophy (Kama-loka and Devachan)
description: Blavatsky’s system divides the human being into seven principles and death into stages. The body goes; the lower vehicles disintegrate in kama-loka, an astral zone where the desire-nature burns itself out and where, Theosophists argued, seance-room "spirits" are usually only the discarded shell. What survives passes into devachan — a long, blissful, essentially subjective rest in which every unfulfilled aspiration is realized — before the ego returns to another incarnation to continue the work.
origin: Blavatsky and the Theosophical Society, New York, London and Adyar (from 1875)

name: Akan (Asamando and the Nsamanfo)
description: The Akan dead cross water to Asamando, the ancestral country — a shadowed mirror of this one — where an old woman, Amokye, receives them at the bank and takes their beads as the toll. Whether they arrive at all depends on the living: the funeral rites are what get a person through, which is why Akan funerals are the largest events a community holds. Those who arrive and are remembered become nsamanfo, ancestors honoured at blackened stools. The okra, the divine spark, returns to Nyame and often comes back into the same matrilineage.
origin: Akan peoples of Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire, especially the Asante (c. 1600 CE onward)

name: Haudenosaunee (The Sky World Road)
description: For ten days after a death the spirit is still present, and the community behaves accordingly: the dead are spoken to, given a portion of the food, and formally released at the Ten Day Feast. Then the spirit travels the Milky Way — the Path of Souls — back to the Sky World the first woman fell from, a journey with ordeals along it and strawberries, sweet water and light at the end. The Condolence, performed by the opposite moiety, is directed at the grieving rather than the dead: it lifts the mourner’s mind so the nation can function again.
origin: Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy, northeastern woodlands (c. 1450 CE onward)
searchText: Death → ten days in which the spirit is present, addressed and fed → the Ten Day Feast, releasing it and distributing belongings → travel along the Milky Way, the Path of Souls, with ordeals and with strawberries and good water, roughly a year → arrival in the Sky World. name: Sámi (Saivo Beneath the Mountain)
description: The Sámi dead live in saivo — a world inside the sacred mountains, or beneath the false bottom of certain double-bottomed lakes, entered through a small hole. It is not a reward and not a punishment: the saivo-people keep tents, herd, hunt and fish exactly as here, and families continue. Alongside it lies Jábmiidáibmu, the realm of the death-goddess Jábmiidáhkku, generally reckoned the bleaker option. The noaidi reaches both by drum, and negotiates with the dead on behalf of the living.
origin: Sámi of Sápmi — northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and the Kola Peninsula
searchText: Death → passage into saivo, inside the sacred mountains or beneath a double-bottomed lake → continuation of ordinary life there with one’s own family, neither rewarded nor punished → remaining reachable, and able to call the living, with the noaidi travelling by drum to negotiate. name: Cārvāka (Lokāyata)
description: India’s materialist school denied the whole apparatus from inside the Indian conversation: no soul separable from the body, no karma, no rebirth, no heaven, no hell, no liberation. Consciousness arises from the elements as intoxication arises from mixed ingredients, and ends when they disperse. Its most quoted line advises borrowing to drink ghee, since the body once burned does not return. Almost nothing of its literature survives — it is known mostly through opponents quoting it in order to refute it.
origin: Indian materialist school (Cārvāka / Lokāyata), attested from c. 600 BCE
